title: Bangladesh | MLPA 2012, ATA 2009 and BFIU Circular 26 AML/CFT Compliance
tagline: Apply Bangladesh's MLPA, ATA, MLP Rules 2019 and BFIU Circular 26: CDD, STRs and CTRs on goAML, sanctions freezing and a programme BFIU would accept.
description:
This quest teaches the anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist and proliferation financing rules that apply to conventional scheduled banks in Bangladesh. It is based on the **Money Laundering Prevention Act 2012** (as amended), the **Anti-Terrorism Act 2009** (as amended, most recently in 2026), the **Money Laundering Prevention Rules 2019**, and the **Bangladesh Financial Intelligence Unit's** Circular 26 for scheduled banks, its guidance on STRs, PEPs and TF/PF, and its later circular letters.

BFIU Circular 26 (paragraph 11.2) requires every bank to give all officers suitable AML/CFT/CPF training, with refreshers, and Rule 6(3) of the MLP Rules 2019 makes training part of each bank's compliance programme. This quest supports that duty for branch, operations, compliance, trade and audit staff, BAMLCOs and managers, at induction and as a refresher.

In five stages you join the AML & CFT Division of a fictional Bangladeshi bank: mapping the law, onboarding customers, reporting on goAML, freezing sanctioned funds and preparing for a BFIU inspection.

The quest builds knowledge and does not replace your bank's own AML/CFT policy and procedures; always follow them and the latest BFIU and Bangladesh Bank instructions.
audience: Branch, account-opening, cash and remittance staff at scheduled banks in Bangladesh who carry out CDD and escalate concerns
BAMLCOs, branch managers and second officers who evaluate referrals and run quarterly AML meetings and self-assessments
AML & CFT Division staff, CAMLCOs and DCAMLCOs who file STRs and CTRs on goAML and run sanctions screening

outcomes: Explain how the MLPA 2012, ATA 2009, MLP Rules 2019 and BFIU Circular 26 fit together, and the offences and penalties they set
Apply Circular 26's CDD triggers, walk-in thresholds, SDD, EDD and PEP/IP rules to real onboarding decisions
Escalate and file STRs and CTRs through the BAMLCO, the AML division and goAML without tipping off
Screen against UN and domestic lists, freeze true matches and report to BFIU by the next working day
Describe the CCC, CAMLCO and BAMLCO roles, self-assessment, independent testing, training and record keeping
Explain the fines and licence sanctions BFIU can impose on banks and responsible staff

cards.title: Day one at Doyel Commercial Bank
cards.setting: AML & CFT Division, Doyel Commercial Bank PLC head office, Motijheel, Dhaka. 9:05 am.

lines.text: You have just joined the AML & CFT Division of Doyel Commercial Bank PLC. A BFIU inspection is expected this quarter, and your mission is to make the bank ready for it.
Welcome! I'm Tahmina Rahman, the bank's CAMLCO. Five stages stand between you and that inspection. We begin with the rulebook.
Arif Hossain, DCAMLCO. I run the division day to day. Agrabad branch in Chattogram has already been on the phone this morning.
(on video) Nusrat Jahan Chowdhury, BAMLCO at Agrabad. A garments supplier paid in a big pile of cash across two counters, then asked my cash officer whether the bank 'tells anyone' about deposits.
So is this an MLPA matter, an ATA matter or a Circular 26 matter? The branch wants one clear answer.
Sometimes all three apply at once. That is why stage one is the map: the laws, the offences and who does what.
Stage one is the Motijheel Archive. Ready to read the rulebook the way a BFIU inspector does?

cards.title: Five layers of Bangladesh's AML/CFT rulebook

scenes.heading: The MLPA 2012
scenes.narration: The Money Laundering Prevention Act 2012 defines money laundering, lists the predicate offences, sets the penalties and gives banks their core duties: know the customer, keep records and report suspicious transactions to BFIU.

scenes.heading: The ATA 2009
scenes.narration: The Anti-Terrorism Act 2009 creates the terrorist financing offence, lets the Government list people and proscribe entities, and gives Bangladesh Bank powers that BFIU exercises. Parliament amended it again in April 2026.

scenes.heading: Rules under the Acts
scenes.narration: The Money Laundering Prevention Rules 2019 add detail: each reporting organisation's compliance programme, customer due diligence, tipping off, record keeping and how BFIU imposes fines.

scenes.heading: BFIU's instructions
scenes.narration: BFIU issues binding instructions under section 23(1)(d) of the MLPA and section 15(1)(d) of the ATA. For scheduled banks the master instruction is BFIU Circular 26 of 16 June 2020, supported by guidance notes and later circular letters.

scenes.heading: Your bank's own layer
scenes.narration: Finally, every bank needs its own AML/CFT policy approved by the board, and instructions that the AML division issues to branches. That is the layer you apply at the counter every day.

cards.title: From statute to branch procedure

cards.title: Real case: what BFIU's own figures tell a branch
cards.body:
In July 2026 BFIU briefed the media on its **Annual Report 2024-25**. Reporting organisations filed **30,199 STRs and SARs** in the year, roughly 74% more than the year before. BFIU sent **199 financial intelligence reports** to investigating and law enforcement agencies and exchanged information **1,329 times** with agencies, regulators and other government bodies.

Two years earlier the total was 14,106. Three lessons follow for bank staff:

- **Your report is one of many.** A thin STR with no clear reason for suspicion is hard for BFIU to use. Quality matters as much as speed.
- **Reports become intelligence.** BFIU turns a small share of reports into intelligence for agencies, and well-documented bank files make that possible.
- **Scrutiny is rising.** At BFIU's May 2026 conference for bank CAMLCOs, BFIU's head urged timely STRs, strong CDD and monitoring, and readiness for Bangladesh's APG mutual evaluation in the 2027-2028 cycle.

cards.title: Splitting the cash
cards.setting: Video call between Motijheel and Agrabad branch, 11:40 am.

lines.text: The supplier rang again. Tomorrow he wants to pay part of his cash here and the rest at our Khatunganj branch 'to save paperwork'.
Splitting cash to slip under a reporting line is structuring. The MLPA's own definition of money laundering includes it.
And my cash officer? He is itching to tell him the bank reports big deposits anyway.
He must not discuss reports with a customer he is uneasy about. Disclosing STR information is an offence under section 6 of the MLPA.
(joining from Sylhet) We see the same pattern in remittance-funded accounts. Where does the duty to report actually come from?
Section 25 of the MLPA, section 16 of the ATA, and Circular 26 paragraph 7 for the steps. Let's test the branch's options.

cards.title: The split deposit
cards.situation: At Agrabad, a supplier deposits Tk 9.5 lakh in cash into his current account in the morning. In the afternoon he returns with Tk 9 lakh more, asks for 'a separate slip so it doesn't look big', mentions he may use another branch tomorrow, and asks whether the bank reports deposits to anyone. His profile shows mostly cheque and transfer receipts. What should the cash officer do?

choices.text: Take both deposits, explain that the bank reports large cash to BFIU so he understands the rules, and move on.
choices.outcome: The day's cash in one account already reaches the CTR level, so it will be reported anyway. But talking about reporting with a customer you are uneasy about risks tipping off, and nobody has escalated the structuring attempt.

choices.text: Take the deposits, make a note of what he said, and report the behaviour in writing to the BAMLCO the same day without discussing reports with him.
choices.outcome: Right. Circular 26 paragraph 7 asks the officer to inform the BAMLCO in writing as soon as something looks suspicious. Nusrat evaluates it, records her view and sends it to the AML division if it stays suspicious. The CTR captures the cash; the STR captures the behaviour.

choices.text: Refuse the afternoon deposit and tell him to bring it on another day.
choices.outcome: Refusing without escalating teaches him to split more carefully and leaves the bank with no record of the attempt. A suspicious attempt is itself reportable under section 25(1)(d).

choices.text: Take the deposits and wait to see whether he really uses the other branch before telling anyone.
choices.outcome: You avoided tipping off, but the duty is to report suspicion promptly and on the bank's own initiative. Waiting for more proof is not the test, and the attempt may already be reportable.

cards.question: A customer's lawyer argues that the bank cannot treat his client's funds as laundered money because the client has never been convicted of fraud. What does the MLPA say?
options: BFIU must first obtain a fraud conviction before it can act
The bank may report only after the police register a case
A charge or conviction for the predicate offence is not a precondition
The MLPA covers only the proceeds of corruption and bribery
cards.explanation: Section 4(5) of the MLPA says being charged with or convicted of the predicate offence is not a precondition for a money laundering charge or penalty. A bank's STR duty rests on suspicion, not on any court outcome.

cards.title: Keep your own rulebook current
cards.body:
- Read the Acts on **bdlaws.minlaw.gov.bd**; the Bengali text is the authoritative version and shows every amendment.
- The ATA was amended in 2012, 2013 and by **Act 28 of 2026** (sections 18 and 20, on measures against listed and proscribed entities).
- Check BFIU's **circular** and **circular letter** pages every month. Letters can change how Circular 26 works in practice.
- When guidance and the circular seem to differ, ask the AML division before acting.

cards.title: Stage one take-aways
items: The MLPA 2012 and the ATA 2009 set the offences and duties; the MLP Rules 2019 and BFIU Circular 26 add the detail for banks.
Money laundering includes structuring and irregular transfers abroad, and needs no prior predicate conviction.
Penalties reach 4 to 12 years for money laundering and 4 to 20 years for terrorist financing, plus heavy fines.
BFIU, housed in Bangladesh Bank, receives STRs and CTRs and supervises banks; it also exercises Bangladesh Bank's ATA powers.
Banks must report suspicion to BFIU promptly and on their own initiative, and never tip the customer off.

cards.prompt: Think of the last time a customer asked you an odd question about how the bank handles large cash. Which law and which Circular 26 paragraph would guide your next step today?

quiz.question: Under which provisions did BFIU issue Circular 26 to scheduled banks?
options: Section 45 of the Bank-Company Act 1991 alone
Rule 6 of the MLP Rules 2019 and section 20A of the ATA 2009
Section 23(1)(d) of the MLPA 2012 and section 15(1)(d) of the ATA 2009
The Bangladesh Bank Order 1972 and the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947
quiz.explanation: Circular 26 states that it was issued under the powers in MLPA section 23(1)(d) and ATA section 15(1)(d), which let BFIU give instructions to reporting organisations.

quiz.question: What sentence range does section 4 of the MLPA set for an individual convicted of money laundering?
options: At least 2 and at most 10 years, with no fine
Up to 7 years' imprisonment or a fine, at the court's choice
At least 4 and at most 20 years of rigorous imprisonment
At least 4 and at most 12 years' imprisonment, plus a fine
quiz.explanation: Section 4(2) sets 4 to 12 years plus a fine of twice the value of the property involved or Tk 10 lakh, whichever is higher. The 4 to 20 year range belongs to the TF offence in section 7 of the ATA.

quiz.question: A trader deposits cash in several smaller amounts on purpose so that no single transaction triggers a report. How does the MLPA treat this?
options: As a breach of internal bank procedure only, to be handled by the branch manager through a warning and staff retraining
As an offence only if the total exceeds Tk 1 crore in a month
As money laundering: conducting or attempting transactions to avoid a reporting requirement is in the Act's definition
As lawful tax planning unless the cash is proved to be stolen
quiz.explanation: The MLPA's definition of money laundering includes carrying out or attempting a transaction so that it escapes reporting under the Act. Circular 26 paragraph 5 also asks banks to watch for structuring.

quiz.question: Which of these is a reporting organisation under section 2 of the MLPA?
options: A private secondary school
A real estate developer
A government hospital
A foreign embassy in Dhaka
quiz.explanation: The MLPA's list includes banks, financial institutions, insurers, money changers, remitters, capital market intermediaries, NGOs/NPOs, cooperative societies, real estate developers, dealers in precious metals or stones, TCSPs, lawyers, notaries and accountants.

quiz.question: Where is BFIU located, and who heads it?
options: In its own office within Bangladesh Bank, headed by a full-time chief of Deputy Governor rank
In the Anti-Corruption Commission, headed by a Commissioner
In the Ministry of Home Affairs as a unit of the police, headed by the Inspector General of Police or an officer he names
In the Ministry of Finance, headed by a Joint Secretary
quiz.explanation: Section 24 of the MLPA sets BFIU up as a separate central agency with its own office inside Bangladesh Bank, which provides staff and funds, and a full-time head of Deputy Governor rank.

quiz.question: A bank's board member asks what fine an entity faces if it commits money laundering. What does section 4(4) of the MLPA provide?
options: At least twice the value of the property involved or Tk 20 lakh, whichever is higher, and its registration may be cancelled
Twice the value of the property, capped at Tk 10 lakh in all cases
Up to Tk 25 lakh, payable to BFIU as an administrative penalty, together with a formal warning letter to the bank's board of directors
A fixed Tk 5 lakh fine, with no effect on registration
quiz.explanation: Section 4(4) sets an entity fine of at least double the property's value or Tk 20 lakh, whichever is higher, and makes its registration liable to cancellation. The Tk 25 lakh cap relates to BFIU's administrative fine under section 25(2).

quiz.question: A Sylhet officer suspects that a customer's account is being used to fund a banned group. Which law sets the bank's duty to report this suspicion?
options: Section 16(1) of the ATA 2009, alongside section 25(1)(d) of the MLPA
Only the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947
Only the bank's own code of conduct
The Penal Code 1860, through the police
quiz.explanation: ATA section 16(1) requires every reporting agency to take due care to detect TF transactions and report suspicious ones to Bangladesh Bank without delay; BFIU exercises those powers. The MLPA's STR duty also covers terrorist financing.

quiz.question: Why does the ATA amendment of April 2026 matter to a bank's AML division?
options: It replaced Circular 26 with a new master circular for banks
It changed the sections on listing and proscription and on measures against listed persons and entities, which feed sanctions screening
It removed terrorist financing from the predicate offences in the MLPA
It abolished BFIU as a separate unit and moved all of its powers over reporting agencies to the Ministry of Home Affairs
quiz.explanation: Act 28 of 2026 amended section 18 (it now also lets the Government ban all activities of an entity) and section 20 on measures against listed or proscribed persons and entities, such as freezing their accounts. BFIU and Circular 26 are unchanged.

quiz.question: At the Agrabad branch, the supplier who split his cash asks the teller directly: 'Will you report me?' What is the best response?
options: Refer him to the AML division head so that he can ask there
Tell him honestly that an STR will be filed, so that he has a fair chance to explain the source of the cash first
Tell him that reports are only filed for amounts above Tk 1 crore
Give no information about any report, finish the service politely and inform the BAMLCO in writing
quiz.explanation: Disclosing information about an STR is prohibited by Rule 18(2) of the MLP Rules 2019 and punishable under section 6 of the MLPA. The officer should not discuss reporting and should escalate to the BAMLCO as Circular 26 paragraph 7 requires.

quiz.question: What do the BFIU figures for FY 2024-25 show?
options: STR filings fell sharply because banks stopped using goAML
About 30,000 STRs and SARs were filed, roughly 74% more than the year before
BFIU received fewer than 5,000 STRs for the first time
All STRs were sent straight to the courts without analysis
quiz.explanation: BFIU's July 2026 press release reported 30,199 STRs/SARs in FY 2024-25, about 74% more than the previous year, and 199 intelligence reports disseminated to agencies.

cards.title: Three customers before lunch
cards.setting: Zindabazar branch, Sylhet. 10:15 am, the account-opening desk is busy.

lines.text: Kamal Uddin Ahmed, branch manager. Three files on my desk and one question each. You're the head office voice today.
One: a returning worker from abroad wants a savings account and plans to deposit his remittances. Two: an upazila chairman wants a fixed deposit for his trust.
Three: a businessman wants a current account. His brother-in-law is a serving deputy minister in another country, and the first credit will come from abroad.
(on the phone) Three different levels of due diligence. Circular 26 paragraph 3 tells us which is which.
My officers know the KYC form. What they don't know is when to stop, who must approve, and what to do if a customer refuses to answer.
Then stage two is for them too. Welcome to the Onboarding Desk.

cards.title: From first contact to ongoing due diligence

scenes.heading: The acceptance policy
scenes.narration: Every bank needs a customer acceptance policy. Under Circular 26 it must bar anonymous, fictitious or numbered accounts, accounts for UN-listed or Government-listed persons and proscribed entities, and any relationship with a shell bank.

scenes.heading: Who counts as a customer
scenes.narration: A customer is not just the account holder. It includes the beneficial owner, a professional intermediary acting for someone, and anyone carrying out a high-value occasional transaction.

scenes.heading: Risk decides the depth
scenes.narration: Each bank assesses its own ML/TF risk using BFIU's risk assessment guidelines. Where risk is high it must apply enhanced due diligence; where risk is shown to be low it may apply simplified due diligence.

scenes.heading: Verify before money moves
scenes.narration: Identity of the customer and the beneficial owner is verified when the relationship starts, or at least before any withdrawal from the new account. For occasional customers it happens during the transaction.

scenes.heading: Due diligence never ends
scenes.narration: The bank builds a transaction profile from the customer's past six to twelve months of activity, watches for change, and refreshes KYC at least every five years for low-risk and every year for high-risk customers.

cards.title: When full CDD is required (Circular 26, para 3.4)
cards.caption: The same triggers appear in Rule 7(2) of the MLP Rules 2019, with BFIU setting the walk-in threshold.

items.label: Starting a relationship
items.detail: Whenever a customer opens an account or begins a business relationship.

items.label: Walk-in, Tk 5 lakh or more
items.detail: An occasional transaction of Tk 5 lakh or above by a non-account holder.

items.label: Occasional wire transfer
items.detail: Any occasional transaction carried out by wire transfer.

items.label: Doubts about old data
items.detail: When there is reason to think earlier identity information is inadequate or wrong.

items.label: Suspicion of ML or TF
items.detail: Do CDD, unless doing so would tip the customer off; then file the STR without it.

cards.title: Simplified due diligence for walk-in customers (para 3.5)
cards.caption: Simplified measures never apply where there is suspicion of ML or TF or a specific higher-risk situation (MLP Rules 2019, rule 10(3)).

items.label: Up to Tk 50,000
items.right: Names and addresses of sender and receiver, and sender's phone number

items.label: Above Tk 50,000, below Tk 5 lakh
items.right: The above plus an attested copy of the sender's or depositor's photo ID

items.label: Tk 5 lakh or more
items.right: Full CDD at the time of the transaction

items.label: Low-risk inclusion accounts
items.left: Social safety net, student, farmer, no-frill

cards.question: Doyel's KYC policy must say how often customer information is refreshed. What does Circular 26 require as a minimum?
options: Every three years for all customers
Every five years for low-risk and every year for high-risk customers
Only when a customer asks to update their address
Every two years for low-risk and every six months for high-risk customers
cards.explanation: Paragraph 3.6(4) sets KYC updates at five-yearly intervals for low-risk and yearly intervals for high-risk customers, plus an update as soon as the bank learns of any change, followed by a fresh risk rating.

cards.title: Enhanced due diligence, PEPs and influential persons
cards.body:
**EDD (para 3.8)** for any high-risk customer means: extra identity information from reliable independent sources; stronger steps to establish the purpose of the account and the source of funds and wealth; closer, regular monitoring; and, where applicable, the **CAMLCO's approval**.

Circular 26 then separates three groups:

- **Foreign PEPs** (para 3.10): people entrusted with prominent public functions by a foreign country. The bank must have a way to identify them, get the **CAMLCO's approval** to open or continue the relationship, and apply EDD in every case.
- **Influential persons, or IPs** (para 3.9): the domestic equivalent. EDD applies when the bank rates the IP as high risk.
- **Heads and senior officials of international organisations** (para 3.11): EDD when rated high risk.

The PEP rules extend to **family members and close associates**. Middle-ranking or junior officials are not PEPs. BFIU's PEP guidance says a PEP or IP should normally stay in that category for at least 12 months after leaving office, depending on risk.

cards.title: SDD, standard CDD or EDD?
cards.prompt: Decide which level of due diligence each case calls for under Circular 26.

items.text: A farmer opens a no-frill account to receive a Government allowance
A walk-in customer sends Tk 30,000 by pay order
A salaried teacher opens a savings account at her local branch
A walk-in customer deposits Tk 6 lakh in cash to a third party's account
A serving foreign deputy minister's sister opens an account
A customer asks for privilege (priority) banking services
A trading company with a director based in a country on FATF's call-for-action list
A customer the bank has rated high risk after a review

lines.text: The businessman is back with his papers. Trade licence, NID, TIN. All clean. The first credit is USD 80,000 from his brother-in-law abroad, 'a gift'.
His brother-in-law is a serving deputy minister in another country. That makes your customer a family member of a foreign PEP.
So I need head office approval? My officer thought only the branch manager signs.
For a foreign PEP relationship, Circular 26 asks for the CAMLCO's approval, not just the manager's. And we need to know where that money really comes from.
He's a good prospect. I don't want to lose him over paperwork.
Nobody is saying no. We are saying 'not yet, and not blind'. Let's work through it.

cards.title: A gift from a minister's relative
cards.situation: A Sylhet businessman wants a current account. His brother-in-law is a serving deputy minister of a foreign country. He says the first credit, USD 80,000 from the brother-in-law, is a family gift to expand his shop. His documents are complete and his declared income is modest. The branch wants to open the account today.

choices.text: Open the account today on standard CDD; the customer himself holds no public office.
choices.outcome: Under paragraph 3.10(4), the PEP measures also apply to a PEP's family members. Treating him as an ordinary customer skips the required approval and source-of-funds checks.

choices.text: Treat him as a PEP family member: collect evidence of the source of funds and wealth, get the CAMLCO's approval before opening, and set up enhanced monitoring.
choices.outcome: Correct. Circular 26 paragraph 3.10 requires a way to identify PEPs, the CAMLCO's approval, EDD under paragraph 3.8 and the same treatment for family members and close associates. If the gift story does not hold up, the AML division considers an STR.

choices.text: Decline the account outright because any link to a foreign politician is too risky.
choices.outcome: Circular 26 does not ban PEP relationships; it requires them to be managed. A blanket refusal without assessment is not a risk-based decision, though declining may be right if EDD fails.

choices.text: Open the account but block foreign inward credits until the brother-in-law leaves office.
choices.outcome: This is an improvised control the rules do not provide for, and it delays the real work: approval, source-of-funds checks and enhanced monitoring. It may also prompt questions that tip the customer off.

cards.back: Someone entrusted with a prominent public function by a foreign country: head of state or government, senior politician, senior official, judge, military officer or state enterprise executive.
The domestic equivalent: someone entrusted with a prominent public function in Bangladesh. EDD applies when the bank rates them high risk.
A director, deputy director or board member of an international organisation. EDD applies when rated high risk.
PEP measures apply to them too; BFIU's guidance treats them as ordinary customers once the PEP has left office, unless risk says otherwise.
People with joint ownership of a company or arrangement with a PEP, or other close business ties. The PEP measures apply to them as well.
BFIU's guidance: keep treating a PEP or IP as such for at least 12 months, longer if the risk remains.

cards.title: Ongoing due diligence loop
cards.caption: Circular 26 paragraphs 3.4(2)-(3) and 3.6(3)-(4). Take care that the customer is not harassed in the process.

items.label: Build the profile
items.detail: Expected activity based on the customer's last 6-12 months of transactions.

items.label: Monitor
items.detail: Compare actual transactions with the profile, manually or by system.

items.label: Investigate change
items.detail: Ask why activity has shifted; amend the profile or raise an STR.

items.label: Refresh KYC
items.detail: Low risk every 5 years, high risk every year, and on any known change.

items.label: Re-rate risk
items.detail: Re-rate the account at once after an update, including moves from low to high.

cards.question: Doyel wants to open a correspondent relationship with a foreign bank. Which step does Circular 26 make essential before the service starts?
options: Approval from the branch manager of the trade services branch
Collecting the specified information and obtaining the CAMLCO's approval
A no-objection letter from the respondent bank's own central bank
A deposit of at least USD 1 million from the respondent bank
cards.explanation: Paragraph 3.13 requires the bank to gather the information in Annex B, understand the respondent's business and get the CAMLCO's approval, be satisfied the respondent is effectively supervised, and never deal with or through shell banks.

cards.title: Real case: BFIU's CAMLCO conference on loan fraud (May 2026)
cards.body:
On 8-9 May 2026 BFIU held a two-day conference in Cox's Bazar for the managing directors and CAMLCOs of scheduled banks. Its theme was strengthening AML/CFT compliance through integrity, governance, digital transformation and collaboration.

BFIU reported that sessions covered recovery of laundered assets, risk-based supervision, **prevention of loan fraud and capital flight**, and preparation for Bangladesh's APG mutual evaluation. Participants singled out lending risks such as **fraudulent entities, fake collateral, diversion of funds and wilful default**, and stressed **robust CDD/KYC**, transaction monitoring and timely STRs.

What this means at the onboarding desk:

- CDD is not only for depositors. Borrowers, guarantors and their beneficial owners need the same rigour.
- Check that a borrower company is real and that its owners are who they say they are.
- Note the purpose of the facility so that later diversion of funds stands out in monitoring.

cards.title: When a customer won't complete CDD
cards.prompt: Put the branch's steps in the order Circular 26 paragraph 3.7 and Rule 11 suggest.
steps: Ask for the missing information and documents and try to verify them from reliable sources
Conclude that satisfactory CDD cannot be completed because the customer will not cooperate or the data is unreliable
Do not open the account, start the relationship or carry out the transaction (or end an existing relationship)
Record the decision and send the details to the AML & CFT Division
The AML division considers an STR and, where needed, alerts other branches

cards.title: Remote onboarding and new products
cards.body:
- **Non-face-to-face customers** (para 3.15): those who open accounts or transact online, through agents or through lawyers or accountants need their own risk assessment and controls. BFIU's e-KYC guidelines and Bangladesh Bank's March 2026 e-KYC guidelines set the remote onboarding rules.
- **New products and technology** (para 3.16): assess ML/TF risk **before** launching internet banking features, cards, e-KYC tools or new payment platforms, not after.
- **Unique customer code (UCIC):** one code for a customer's many accounts makes monitoring easier.

cards.title: Stage two take-aways
items: Circular 26 bars anonymous, fictitious and numbered accounts, listed or proscribed customers and shell banks.
Full CDD applies when a relationship starts, for walk-in transactions of Tk 5 lakh or more, for occasional wires, on doubts, and on suspicion.
Walk-in SDD tiers: up to Tk 50,000 basic details; above that and below Tk 5 lakh, add an attested photo ID copy.
Refresh KYC every five years for low-risk and every year for high-risk customers, and re-rate after each update.
Foreign PEPs always need EDD and the CAMLCO's approval; IPs and international organisation heads need EDD when high risk.
If CDD cannot be completed, do not open or continue the relationship, inform the AML division and consider an STR.

cards.prompt: Pick one customer type your branch onboards every week. Which Circular 26 trigger, due diligence level and approval route applies, and where could a busy officer cut a corner?

quiz.question: A walk-in customer at Doyel's Khulna branch wants to deposit Tk 6 lakh in cash into a supplier's account. What does Circular 26 require?
options: Full CDD on the walk-in customer at the time of the transaction
Only the depositor's name and phone number
Nothing, because the money goes into an existing account
An attested photo ID copy, but no other due diligence
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 3.4(1)(b) requires CDD for occasional walk-in transactions of Tk 5 lakh or more. The lighter SDD tiers in paragraph 3.5 apply only below Tk 5 lakh.

quiz.question: For a walk-in transaction of Tk 40,000, what must the branch collect at a minimum?
options: An attested photo ID copy of the receiver only
Full CDD, including source of funds and a KYC profile
No information, because the amount is under Tk 50,000
Names and addresses of the sender and receiver, and the sender's phone number
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 3.5(a) sets the minimum for walk-in transactions up to Tk 50,000: the names and addresses of applicant and beneficiary and the applicant's phone number.

quiz.question: When must the identity of a new account holder normally be verified?
options: Only when the account balance first exceeds Tk 10 lakh
Within six months of opening, during the first periodic KYC review, as long as no foreign remittance arrives
Only if the customer later receives a foreign remittance
When the relationship is set up, or at the latest before any withdrawal from the new account
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 3.4(4) and Rule 8 require verification at or before the start of the relationship, or after opening but before money is withdrawn. Where risk is low and controls exist, it may follow as soon as practicable.

quiz.question: What does paragraph 3.8 list as part of enhanced due diligence?
options: A higher minimum balance, a local guarantor, a larger service charge and a signed declaration that the customer is not a politician
Extra identity data from reliable sources, stronger checks on purpose and source of funds, closer monitoring and, where applicable, CAMLCO approval
Collecting a second photograph and a utility bill for every account
A personal visit by the branch manager to the customer's home
quiz.explanation: EDD under paragraph 3.8 means additional information from reliable independent sources, more on the purpose and source of funds, more frequent monitoring and, where applicable, the CAMLCO's approval.

quiz.question: A senior judge of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh opens an account. How should the bank classify the customer under Circular 26?
options: As a head of an international organisation
As a foreign PEP, requiring the CAMLCO's approval and enhanced due diligence in every case, whatever the risk rating
As an influential person (IP), applying EDD if the bank rates the relationship high risk
As an ordinary customer, because judges are exempt
quiz.explanation: Circular 26 uses 'influential persons' for people entrusted with prominent public functions domestically, such as senior judicial officials, and requires EDD when they are high risk (para 3.9). 'PEP' in the circular means foreign PEPs.

quiz.question: A foreign PEP's business partner, who co-owns a company with the PEP, applies for an account. What applies?
options: The PEP measures, because they extend to close associates
Simplified CDD, since the PEP is not the account holder
Standard CDD only, since the partner holds no office
Nothing extra unless the partner is also a public official
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 3.10(4) applies the PEP instructions to family members and close associates; BFIU's PEP guidance describes joint ownership of an entity with a PEP as a close-associate link.

quiz.question: Which of these may Doyel apply simplified due diligence to, if its risk assessment supports it?
options: A school student's account opened for financial inclusion
A company owned through a trust abroad
A customer whose earlier ID documents now look forged
A privilege banking customer with large deposits
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 3.5(c) allows SDD for low-risk financial inclusion accounts such as social safety net, school student, farmer and no-frill accounts. Privilege banking requires EDD under paragraph 3.6(5).

quiz.question: An officer asks a customer about the source of a sudden large deposit, and the customer seems ready to vanish if questioned further. The officer already suspects laundering. What does the MLP Rules 2019 say?
options: Close the account at once and explain the reason to the customer
If CDD would alert the customer, skip it and file an STR with BFIU instead
Complete full CDD first, even if the customer is alerted
Wait for the next periodic KYC review before taking action
quiz.explanation: Rule 12 of the MLP Rules 2019 and Circular 26 paragraph 3.4(1)(e) say that where performing CDD may tip off the customer, the bank should not perform it and should file an STR.

quiz.question: Which is prohibited outright by Circular 26's customer acceptance rules?
options: Accounts for customers who live outside the branch's district
Any banking relationship with a shell bank
Accounts for foreign nationals working in Bangladesh
Accounts for charities registered with the Government
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 2 bars anonymous, fictitious and numbered accounts, accounts for listed or proscribed persons and entities, and any relationship with a shell bank. Foreign nationals and NGOs can be customers with the right due diligence.

quiz.question: A customer refuses to explain the ownership structure of his company, and the documents he gives cannot be verified. What should the branch do?
options: Open the account if the branch manager signs a waiver
Open the account on simplified due diligence, flag it for review after a year, and ask for the documents again at that point
Not open the account, record the reasons, inform the AML division and consider an STR
Ask the customer to sign a declaration and proceed
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 3.7 and Rule 11 say that if satisfactory CDD cannot be completed, the bank should not open the account or start the relationship (or should end it), send the information to the AML division and consider an STR.

sessions.title: Monitoring, STRs, CTRs and goAML
sessions.summary: Follow the STR route from branch officer to BAMLCO to the AML division and goAML, file CTRs correctly with their exceptions, track BFIU's 2024-2026 circular letter changes, and avoid tipping off.
objectives: Describe the identify-evaluate-disclose STR process and each person's role
Apply the CTR threshold, deadline and exceptions in Circular 26 paragraph 6
Explain tipping off, its penalty and the good-faith protection in the MLPA
Document reporting decisions in a way BFIU and inspectors can follow

cards.title: The control room on CTR day
cards.setting: AML & CFT Division, Motijheel. The 19th of the month, 4:30 pm.

lines.text: Two days to the CTR deadline, 214 open monitoring alerts, and three branch referrals waiting for a decision. Welcome to the goAML Control Room.
On the screen: a salaried customer's account in Khulna has received 40 transfers from unrelated people this week, each withdrawn at an ATM within hours.
The system flagged it as unusual. Unusual is not yet suspicious. Our job is to work out which it is, fast, and write it up properly.
(on the line) Agrabad here. I have evaluated the supplier who split his cash. My written note is ready to send up to you.
Good. Remember, the division can file an STR even when a branch didn't flag anything, and a branch flag doesn't automatically become one. Evidence decides.
Let's walk the whole chain, from a cash officer's doubt to a report on goAML.

scenes.heading: Identify
scenes.narration: It starts when someone notices something unusual: a mismatch with the KYC profile, a monitoring alert or a red flag. BFIU's STR guidance says unusual is only a reason to ask more questions, and any employee can raise it.

scenes.heading: Evaluate at the branch
scenes.narration: The officer tells the BAMLCO in writing at once. The BAMLCO analyses the facts, writes down the findings and, if the activity still looks suspicious, sends it with supporting documents to the AML division without delay.

scenes.heading: Review at head office
scenes.narration: The AML & CFT Division checks that the case is complete and adds anything else it knows. It can also raise its own STR when a branch did not flag the activity.

scenes.heading: Disclose on goAML
scenes.narration: The division files the STR or SAR to BFIU without delay through goAML web, following the goAML manual. It keeps the case information until BFIU says otherwise.

scenes.heading: Stay silent
scenes.narration: Throughout, nobody tells the customer or any outsider that a report is being considered or has been made. That is tipping off, and it is an offence.

cards.title: The STR route at Doyel (Circular 26, para 7)

items.label: Officer spots it
items.detail: Any officer alert to unusual activity, using MLPA s.2(z) and ATA s.2(16) definitions.

items.label: Written note to BAMLCO
items.detail: Sent at once, in writing, with what was seen and why it matters.

items.label: BAMLCO evaluates
items.detail: Analyses promptly, records observations, sends suspicious cases up with documents.

items.label: AML division reviews
items.detail: Checks completeness, adds information, decides; may report on its own initiative.

items.label: STR filed on goAML
items.detail: Submitted to BFIU without delay; case data kept until BFIU instructs.

cards.title: Escalate or explain?
cards.prompt: Decide whether each situation should go to the BAMLCO as possible suspicion, or can be explained, documented and monitored.

items.text: Many small transfers from unrelated people, withdrawn by ATM within hours
A customer asks how much cash he can deposit before the bank 'files anything'
A student's account suddenly receives large business payments
A trader's import invoices are far above normal market prices for the goods
A salaried customer receives her annual festival bonus
A known exporter's receipts rise in the peak season, matching shipping documents
A pensioner withdraws more cash before a family wedding and says so

cards.question: Doyel's Khulna branch must decide whether a cash deposit belongs in the CTR. Which rule applies under Circular 26 paragraph 6?
options: Any single cash deposit of Tk 5 lakh or more
Total cash deposits or withdrawals of Tk 10 lakh or more in one account in one day
Cash deposits of Tk 10 lakh or more in a month across all of a customer's accounts
Only cash withdrawals of Tk 20 lakh or more in a single transaction
cards.explanation: Paragraph 6(1) covers cash deposited or withdrawn (including online and ATM) in one account on a single day, in one or more transactions, of Tk 10 lakh or more or the equivalent in foreign currency.

cards.title: Cash transaction reports (para 6)
cards.body:
Each month branches review the previous month's transactions. Where cash deposits or withdrawals in **one account on one day** reach **Tk 10 lakh or more** (or the foreign currency equivalent), including online and ATM cash, the AML division reports them to BFIU as a CTR.

- **Deadline:** the month's CTR goes in by the **21st of the following month**, through **goAML web**, following the goAML manual.
- **Review:** CTR data is reviewed regularly; anything suspicious becomes an STR.
- **Branch copy:** each branch keeps its monthly CTR data, or can access it if held centrally.

**Exceptions:**

- Cash **deposits** into Government, state-owned, semi-government or autonomous bodies' accounts need no CTR, but **withdrawals** do.
- The same applies to accounts that collect fees for educational institutions and Government utility bills.
- Inter-bank and inter-branch cash movements need no CTR.

A CTR is not an accusation. It is a routine report, and it never replaces an STR when there is suspicion.

cards.title: Real changes to CTR and monitoring rules
cards.caption: All from BFIU circular letters to scheduled banks published on bfiu.org.bd. Always check the latest letters before you rely on a rule.

items.label: Circular 26 issued
items.detail: Monthly CTRs by the 21st via goAML; the master circular for banks.

items.label: Deposits taken out
items.detail: Circular letter 1: cash deposits no longer included in CTRs, from August 2024.

items.label: Deposits back in
items.detail: Circular letter 2 cancelled the August change with immediate effect.

items.label: Weekly CTRs ordered
items.detail: From 11 January 2026, CTRs to be filed within 3 working days after each week.

items.label: Monitoring tightened
items.detail: Circular letter 2 told banks to strengthen transaction monitoring and file STRs without delay.

items.label: Back to monthly
items.detail: Circular letter 4 cancelled weekly filing; monthly CTRs under Circular 26 from March 2026.

cards.front: Myth: it's only tipping off if I say 'we filed an STR'.
cards.back: Fact: hinting, or questioning a customer so hard that he realises he is under suspicion, can also tip him off, as BFIU's STR guidance warns.

cards.front: Myth: once a customer leaves the bank, I can tell him.
cards.back: Fact: section 6 of the MLPA bars misuse or disclosure of such information during and after employment.
Up to 2 years' imprisonment, a fine of up to Tk 50,000, or both (MLPA section 6(3)).

cards.front: Which rule bans disclosing STR information?
cards.back: Rule 18(2) of the MLP Rules 2019; breach is punishable under section 6 of the MLPA.

cards.front: If CDD might alert the customer?
cards.back: Do not perform it. File the STR instead (Rule 12 and Circular 26 para 3.4).

cards.front: Am I protected if I report in good faith?
cards.back: Yes. Section 28 of the MLPA bars legal action against a reporting organisation or its staff for acts done in good faith under the Act.

cards.title: A phone call too far
cards.setting: Khulna branch, 10:00 am, three days later.

lines.text: The Khulna account with 40 transfers a week is now with the AML division. The branch's relationship officer is uneasy.
(visiting Khulna) The relationship officer wants to call the customer and ask him straight out who all these senders are.
On a normal account, asking about unexpected activity is part of ongoing due diligence. Here we already suspect a mule account.
If we ask, he'll know. If we don't, we look careless.
The rules settle this for us. If we suspect laundering and CDD would tip him off, we don't do the CDD. We report.
Let's see how each option plays out.

cards.title: The mule account
cards.situation: A Khulna customer's salary account receives about 40 small transfers a week from unrelated senders, each withdrawn by ATM within hours. Monitoring flagged it, the BAMLCO found no business reason and sent it up, and the AML division suspects the account is being used to move fraud proceeds. A relationship officer proposes calling the customer to ask who the senders are.

choices.text: Call the customer, explain that the bank is worried about the transfers, and ask for documents.
choices.outcome: Telling the customer the bank is worried, while it already suspects laundering, is likely to alert him. Funds may vanish and the investigation is harmed.

choices.text: File the STR on goAML without delay and without contacting the customer, document the decision, and keep monitoring.
choices.outcome: Correct. Rule 12 and Circular 26 paragraph 3.4(1)(e) say that where CDD may tip off the customer, the bank should report without performing it. The division records its reasons, as BFIU's STR guidance expects, and keeps the case information until BFIU instructs otherwise.

choices.text: Freeze the account at once on the bank's own authority and tell the customer to visit the branch.
choices.outcome: A bank cannot freeze an ordinary customer's account on suspicion alone; suspension orders come from BFIU (MLPA s.23(1)(c)). Summoning the customer also risks tipping him off.

choices.text: Wait one more month to collect stronger evidence before reporting.
choices.outcome: The STR duty is to report promptly once there is suspicion. Waiting adds risk, and BFIU can ask for more information later.

cards.title: From transactions to a filed STR
cards.caption: Circular 26 paragraph 5 asks banks to give complex, unusual and pointless transactions special attention, using BFIU's STR and TBML guidance.

items.label: All transactions
items.detail: Monitored manually and by system, including FX and electronic payments.

items.label: Alerts and red flags
items.detail: Profile mismatches, structuring, complex or pointless transactions.

items.label: Unusual activity
items.detail: Something that needs questions answered; not yet suspicious.

items.label: Reasonable suspicion
items.detail: No convincing explanation; grounds to suspect ML or TF remain.

items.label: STR on goAML
items.detail: Filed by the AML division to BFIU without delay.

cards.question: A branch did not flag a series of trade payments, but the AML division's own review finds them suspicious. What should happen?
options: Nothing, because only the branch can start an STR
Send the case back to the branch to file the STR
The AML division files the STR itself
Wait until the branch's next quarterly AML meeting
cards.explanation: Circular 26 paragraph 7(5) and BFIU's STR guidance say the AML division must file an STR where it finds a transaction or activity suspicious, even if the branch did not identify it.

cards.title: How Doyel documents an STR decision
cards.body:
BFIU's STR guidance expects banks to keep records that show how each concern was handled. For the Khulna mule account, Arif's file note covers:

- **What came in:** the monitoring alert and the BAMLCO's written evaluation, with dates.
- **What was checked:** the KYC profile (salaried, modest income), six months of history, the 40 senders and the ATM locations.
- **Why it is suspicious:** pass-through pattern, no business purpose, activity far beyond the profile.
- **The decision:** STR filed on goAML on the same day, with the reference number.
- **Why no CDD call:** a call would probably have tipped off the customer (Rule 12).
- **What next:** enhanced monitoring, and no change to the relationship until the bank decides otherwise, keeping BFIU's instructions in mind.

A file like this protects staff who acted in good faith and shows an inspector that the bank's process works. It also helps when BFIU or an investigating agency asks for documents, because the records are already in order.

cards.title: Reports and records
cards.prompt: Match each report or record to what it is for.

pairs.right: Report of a transaction or attempted transaction that the bank suspects is linked to ML or TF.
Report of suspicious activity or behaviour, even where no transaction has taken place.
Routine monthly report of cash deposits or withdrawals of Tk 10 lakh or more in one account in a day.
The branch's record of its analysis before sending a suspicious case to head office.
Head office record of why a report was or was not filed, kept for inspectors and BFIU.

cards.title: Writing an STR BFIU can use
cards.body:
- **Lead with the reason for suspicion** in plain words, not just 'unusual transactions'.
- **Name the people and accounts** involved, with dates, amounts and channels.
- **Explain the mismatch:** what the profile says against what actually happened.
- **Attach the evidence:** KYC, statements, vouchers, trade documents.
- **Never** mention the STR in customer letters, notes the customer can see or calls with the customer.

cards.title: Stage three take-aways
items: An STR moves from officer to BAMLCO (in writing) to the AML division, which files it to BFIU on goAML without delay.
The AML division must file an STR on its own when it finds suspicion, even if the branch did not flag it.
CTRs cover cash of Tk 10 lakh or more in one account in a day and are filed monthly by the 21st on goAML.
BFIU has changed CTR details several times by circular letter since 2024, so always check the latest letters.
Tipping off is punishable by up to 2 years or Tk 50,000; if CDD would tip off, report without doing it.

cards.prompt: Recall an alert or referral you handled recently. Could someone at BFIU understand from your notes alone why you were, or were not, suspicious?

quiz.question: Under Circular 26, what must a branch officer do first on spotting a suspicious transaction?
options: Ask the customer to explain the transaction in writing
File the STR directly on goAML from the branch
Inform the BAMLCO in writing at once
Wait for the next quarterly branch AML meeting
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 7(3) requires the officer to inform the BAMLCO in writing as soon as a suspicious transaction or activity is identified. The AML division, not the branch, files on goAML.

quiz.question: By when must a month's CTR reach BFIU under Circular 26 as now applied?
options: By the end of the following quarter, by email
By the 7th of the following month, on paper
By the 21st of the following month, through goAML web
Within 3 working days after the end of each week
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 6(2) sets the 21st of the next month via goAML. BFIU briefly ordered weekly filing from January 2026 but cancelled that from March 2026, restoring the Circular 26 schedule.

quiz.question: A municipality's account receives Tk 15 lakh in cash deposits one day and Tk 12 lakh is withdrawn in cash the next day. What goes into the CTR?
options: Neither, because Government bodies are fully exempt
Only the Tk 12 lakh withdrawal
Only the Tk 15 lakh deposit
Both the deposit and the withdrawal
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 6(5) exempts cash deposits into Government, local government, state-owned, semi-government and autonomous bodies' accounts, but cash withdrawals from those accounts must be reported.

quiz.question: What does BFIU's STR guidance list as the three stages of reporting?
options: Identification, evaluation and disclosure
Onboarding, monitoring and closure
Detection, freezing and prosecution
Alerting, interviewing and confirming
quiz.explanation: Section C of the guidance describes identification of unusual activity, evaluation (at branch level by the BAMLCO and then at head office) and disclosure to BFIU on goAML.

quiz.question: What maximum penalty does the MLPA set for tipping off?
options: Up to 2 years' imprisonment, a fine of up to Tk 50,000, or both
A fixed fine of Tk 25 lakh on the officer
A warning letter for a first offence
Up to 12 years' imprisonment and a fine of twice the amount involved or Tk 10 lakh, whichever is higher
quiz.explanation: Section 6(3) of the MLPA sets up to 2 years, a fine of up to Tk 50,000, or both, for disclosing investigation-related information or misusing information obtained under the Act.

quiz.question: After filing an STR, how long must Doyel keep the information about it?
options: Until the customer closes the account
Until BFIU gives a further instruction
Only until BFIU acknowledges receipt on goAML
For exactly one year from filing
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 7(6) and BFIU's STR guidance require the bank to keep STR information until BFIU instructs otherwise, on top of the general five-year record rules.

quiz.question: Which transfers are outside the CTR requirement altogether?
options: Inter-bank and inter-branch cash movements
Cash withdrawals by Government bodies
Cash deposited at an ATM by a customer
Foreign currency cash deposits by individuals
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 6(7) says no CTR is needed for inter-bank and inter-branch cash transactions. ATM and foreign currency cash are expressly included in the threshold calculation.

quiz.question: A relationship officer believes that asking a suspected mule-account holder about his transfers would alert him. What should the bank do?
options: Ask the customer's employer to explain the transfers
Report the suspicion to BFIU without carrying out that CDD step
Close the account without filing anything
Carry out the CDD call anyway, because CDD is always mandatory and must be finished before any report
quiz.explanation: Rule 12 of the MLP Rules 2019 and Circular 26 paragraph 3.4(1)(e) say that where CDD may tip off a suspected customer, the bank should not perform it and should file an STR.

quiz.question: Which protection does section 28 of the MLPA give bank staff?
options: Immunity from any action, even if they knowingly helped a customer launder money, as long as an STR was filed later
A right to refuse to file STRs that may upset customers
Protection only for CAMLCOs, not for branch staff
No civil, criminal or administrative action can be brought against them for acts done in good faith under the Act or rules
quiz.explanation: Section 28 bars proceedings against the Government, BFIU, investigating agencies, reporting organisations, their boards and staff for acts done in good faith under the Act or rules. It does not protect wrongdoing.

quiz.question: Circular 26 paragraph 5 asks banks to be alert to which activity named in the MLPA's definition of money laundering?
options: Opening several accounts for different family members
Using internet banking from abroad
Paying utility bills in cash at the branch
Structuring transactions to avoid reporting requirements
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 5(3) asks banks to watch for structuring, the activity in the MLPA's definition where transactions are conducted or attempted so as to avoid reporting.

sessions.title: Terrorist and Proliferation Financing: Screening and Freezing
sessions.summary: Apply the ATA 2009 (as amended in 2026) and Circular 26 paragraph 10: the TF offence, domestic listing and proscription, UN sanctions regimes, screening, freezing and next-working-day reporting, false positives, BFIU suspension orders and wire transfer information.
objectives: Explain the TF offence, its penalties and the bank's duties under ATA sections 16 and 20A
Screen customers, owners and transactions against UN and domestic lists
Freeze and report a true match to BFIU by the next working day and handle false positives
Respond to media reports, BFIU suspension orders and domestic proscriptions

cards.title: A name in the news
cards.setting: AML & CFT Division, Motijheel. 8:50 am, the morning papers are on the table.

lines.text: A news site reports that a local charity is linked to a banned militant group. The charity banks with our Sylhet branch.
(on the phone) I've seen it. Their account had two cash deposits yesterday. Do I stop everything?
First, check: is the charity, or anyone controlling it, on the UN lists or the Government's list of listed and proscribed entities?
And whatever the screening shows, Circular 26 says that when the media reports TF or PF links, we send BFIU the account details without delay.
Screening, freezing, reporting. Each has its own clock. My officers mix them up.
Then stage four is the Sanctions Gate. Let's get the clocks right.

cards.title: How Bangladesh fights terrorist and proliferation financing

scenes.heading: The offence
scenes.narration: Under section 7 of the ATA it is an offence to provide, receive, collect or arrange money, services or property, from any source, intending or knowing it will be used for terrorist acts or by a terrorist person or entity. The funds need not be used in an actual attack.

scenes.heading: Domestic listing
scenes.narration: Under section 18 the Government, on reasonable grounds, can list a person or proscribe an entity by gazette, and since the April 2026 amendment can ban all of an entity's activities. Section 20 then requires its accounts to be frozen.

scenes.heading: UN sanctions
scenes.narration: Section 20A brings in UN Security Council resolution 1267 and its successors and resolution 1373. BFIU's guidance adds the proliferation regimes, including resolution 1718 on North Korea and the Iran resolutions.

scenes.heading: Who does what
scenes.narration: The Ministry of Foreign Affairs gives effect to UN listings through SROs, national committees coordinate, and BFIU directs reporting organisations under the ATA.

scenes.heading: The bank's part
scenes.narration: Each bank keeps the lists electronically, screens customers and transactions, stops matched transactions at once and reports to BFIU by the next working day, keeping records of false positives.

cards.title: From screening to freezing (Circular 26, para 10)
cards.caption: The bank's board must approve the TF/PF procedure and staff instructions (para 10(1)); BFIU's TF/PF guidance adds real-time screening of cross-border payments.

items.label: Keep lists current
items.detail: UN and Government lists held electronically and checked regularly for updates.

items.label: Screen everyone
items.detail: Customers, beneficial owners, controlled or associated parties and transactions.

items.label: Investigate the hit
items.detail: Compare identifiers; record false positives with the reasons.

items.label: Stop at once
items.detail: Freeze or suspend the account or transaction immediately on a true match.

items.label: Report to BFIU
items.detail: Full details by the next working day.

cards.title: Sanctions regimes a bank must cover
cards.prompt: Match each UN Security Council regime, as listed in BFIU's TF/PF guidance, to its focus.

pairs.right: Al-Qaida and ISIL (Da'esh): UN-listed individuals and entities.
Countries freeze terrorist funds and list terrorists themselves; basis for domestic listing.
Keeping weapons of mass destruction away from non-state actors.
Proliferation sanctions on North Korea (DPRK).
Proliferation sanctions related to Iran.

cards.question: Doyel's screening system finds a customer whose name, date of birth and passport number match a UN-listed person. By when must BFIU be told?
options: Within 30 days, in the next CTR
By the next working day, with full details
At the next half-yearly CCC report
Only after a court confirms the match
cards.explanation: Circular 26 paragraph 10(4) requires the bank to stop the account's or transaction's activity at once on identification and to send BFIU full details by the next working day.

cards.title: TF penalties and the bank's duties under the ATA
cards.body:
**For individuals (s.7(3)):** 4 to 20 years' rigorous imprisonment plus a fine of twice the value of the property or Tk 10 lakh, whichever is higher.

**For entities (s.7(4)):** action under section 18, a fine of three times the value or Tk 50 lakh, whichever is higher, and its head faces 4 to 20 years unless they prove the offence happened without their knowledge or despite their efforts.

**For reporting agencies (s.16):** take due care to prevent and detect TF transactions and report suspicion to Bangladesh Bank without delay; the board (or CEO) must approve staff instructions. Failure can bring a fine of up to **Tk 25 lakh** and suspension of a branch's or the bank's licence; a chair or CEO who fails can be fined up to Tk 25 lakh and removed.

**Failing to freeze (s.20A(5)):** a fine of Tk 5 lakh to Tk 25 lakh, or twice the suspected funds, whichever is higher, plus possible licence suspension.

cards.title: TF/PF red flag or ordinary activity?

items.text: Media report links the account holder to a proscribed organisation
Charity receives cash from unknown donors and sends it to a conflict area
Importer's goods could be used in weapons and the end user is unclear
Shell company in the payment chain hides who is behind a trade deal
Name partly matches a listed person, but date of birth and nationality differ
Garment exporter receives payment from a long-standing European buyer
A school deposits monthly tuition fees in line with its usual pattern

items.label: TF prison term
items.detail: Rigorous imprisonment for individuals under ATA section 7(3).

items.label: Report a sanctions match
items.detail: Full details to BFIU after the bank stops the transaction (Circular 26 para 10(4)).

items.label: Fine for failing to freeze
items.detail: Or twice the suspected funds if higher (ATA section 20A(5)).

items.label: BFIU suspension order
items.detail: Under MLPA s.23(1)(c), renewable 30 days at a time, up to 7 times.

lines.text: Good news: the charity is not on any list. Different problem: a remittance for a farmer here has hit a UN list. Same first and last name.
Name alone is not a match. What do the other identifiers say?
Listed person: different nationality, born twenty years earlier. Our farmer has an NID and has banked with us for a decade.
Then it is probably a false positive. But 'probably' needs to be written down, approved and kept.
And the charity story? Nothing on the lists, so do we just carry on?
Not quite. Let's take both decisions one at a time.

cards.title: The charity in the headlines
cards.situation: A news site reports that a charity banking at Doyel's Sylhet branch has links to a proscribed militant group. Screening shows neither the charity nor its trustees on any UN or Government list. The account received two unexplained cash deposits yesterday and has a transfer request pending today.

choices.text: Carry on as normal; nothing is on the lists, so the bank has no duty.
choices.outcome: Circular 26 paragraph 10(2) requires the bank to send BFIU detailed information without delay whenever the media reports TF or PF links to a person or entity holding an account. The list result does not cancel that duty.

choices.text: Send BFIU the account details without delay, review the account for an STR, apply enhanced monitoring and hold the transfer for review under the bank's procedures.
choices.outcome: Correct. The media-report duty applies, the unexplained cash adds suspicion for an STR under ATA s.16(1), and the AML division can now look closely at the pending transfer. A full freeze needs a listing or a BFIU order.

choices.text: Freeze the account permanently and tell the trustees why.
choices.outcome: There is no listing or BFIU order yet, so a permanent freeze has no basis, and telling the trustees risks tipping them off.

choices.text: Ask the trustees to confirm in writing that they have no links to the group.
choices.outcome: A written denial adds little and may alert them. The bank should report and monitor, not ask the subjects to clear themselves.

cards.back: A freeze taken on available information that later checks show was wrong, such as mistaken identity. Records must be kept (Circular 26 para 10(4)).
BFIU can order an account suspended or frozen for up to 30 days where it suspects crime proceeds; it can renew this 30 days at a time, up to 7 times.
After a BFIU suspension order, banks must tell BFIU without delay about the balance and other related accounts (BFIU Circular Letter 5 of August 2026).
BFIU can fine the bank at least the balance of the account involved (MLPA s.23(6)).
Under ATA s.18 the Government lists individuals and proscribes entities by gazette.
For USD 1,000 or more, accurate, verified originator details travel with the payment (Circular 26 para 9).

items.label: Main danger
items.left: Funds reaching terrorists or their acts
items.right: Funds or goods helping build weapons of mass destruction

items.label: Domestic lists
items.right: UN lists given effect through MoFA SROs

items.label: Typical red flags
items.right: Dual-use goods, unclear end users, front companies

items.label: Bank's action on a match
items.left: Stop at once; report BFIU by next working day
items.right: Same: stop at once; report BFIU by next working day

cards.question: In August 2023 the Government banned the activities of the militant group 'Jama'atul Ansar Fil Hindal Sharqiya'. What did BFIU then instruct reporting organisations to do?
options: Report the group's transactions in the next monthly CTR
Freeze any account of the group under ATA section 20(1)(b), stop any business relationship and inform BFIU
Close the group's accounts and pay the balance to its members
Wait for a UN listing before taking any action
cards.explanation: BFIU Circular Letter 01 of 21 August 2023 told all reporting organisations to freeze any account of the group under section 20(1)(b) of the ATA, stop any business relationship and inform BFIU, using its powers under section 15(1)(d).

cards.title: Real case: a domestic proscription reaches the banks (2023)
cards.body:
On **9 August 2023** the Government of Bangladesh, by gazette notification, banned the activities of the militant group **'Jama'atul Ansar Fil Hindal Sharqiya'** as a threat to public security.

On **21 August 2023** BFIU issued **Circular Letter 01** to every kind of reporting organisation, from scheduled banks and insurers to real estate developers, lawyers and accountants. It instructed them to **freeze** any account of the group under section 20(1)(b) of the ATA, **end** any business relationship, and **inform BFIU**, effective at once.

Lessons for Doyel:

- Domestic proscriptions arrive by gazette and BFIU letter, not only through UN list updates. Your screening lists must take them in quickly.
- Screening must catch the group's accounts under other names and those of people acting for it.
- Freezing is immediate; the paperwork follows.

cards.title: Make screening work in practice
cards.body:
- Update lists **electronically** and promptly; a stale list is a compliance failure.
- Screen **beneficial owners, controllers and associates**, not just account names.
- Use identifiers (date of birth, nationality, ID numbers) to clear or confirm hits, and **write down** why.
- Watch the news: a media report of TF/PF links to an account holder triggers a report to BFIU without delay.
- For cross-border wires of USD 1,000 or more, check that verified originator details are present.

cards.title: Stage four take-aways
items: The ATA makes TF punishable by 4 to 20 years' rigorous imprisonment; the funds need not be used in an actual act.
The Government lists persons and proscribes entities under ATA s.18; s.20A brings in UN resolutions 1267 and 1373.
Banks screen customers, owners and transactions against current UN and domestic lists held electronically.
On a true match: stop at once and report to BFIU with full details by the next working day; record false positives.
Media reports of TF/PF links to an account holder must be reported to BFIU without delay.
Failing to freeze can cost Tk 5 to 25 lakh or twice the funds, and a branch or bank licence.

cards.prompt: How quickly would a new domestic proscription announced by gazette reach your bank's screening list, and who would check that it did?

quiz.question: What must the prosecution show to prove terrorist financing under section 7 of the ATA?
options: That the funds came from an illegal source such as smuggling
That the accused is a member of a proscribed organisation
That funds or property were provided or collected with intent or knowledge that they would be used for terrorism or by a terrorist person or entity
That the funds were actually used in a completed terrorist attack, and that the accused knew which attack they would pay for
quiz.explanation: Section 7(1) covers lawful or unlawful sources, and section 7(2) says it is not necessary to show the funds were actually used in, or linked to, a specific terrorist act.

quiz.question: Who lists individuals and proscribes entities linked to terrorism under section 18 of the ATA?
options: Each bank's board, by resolution
The Government, by gazette notification
The High Court Division, on a police application
BFIU, by circular letter
quiz.explanation: Section 18 empowers the Government, on reasonable grounds, to list a person or proscribe an entity by gazette notification. BFIU then directs reporting organisations.

quiz.question: What did the Anti-Terrorism (Amendment) Act 2026 add to section 18?
options: Power for the Government to ban all activities of an entity
Power for banks to list customers as terrorists
A 90-day deadline for banks to report sanctions matches
A rule that UN listings no longer apply in Bangladesh
quiz.explanation: Act 28 of 2026 added words to section 18(1) allowing the Government to ban all of an entity's activities, and it also amended section 20 on measures against listed or proscribed persons and entities.

quiz.question: A screening hit turns out to be a different person with the same name. What must the bank keep?
options: A report to BFIU within 30 days for every partial name hit
A record of the false positive and how it was resolved
Nothing, because only true matches are recorded
A copy of the customer's consent to be screened
quiz.explanation: Circular 26 paragraph 10(4) requires banks to keep information on false positives, and BFIU's TF/PF guidance asks for an audit trail of all monitoring, including false positives.

quiz.question: Which resolution is the basis for countries' own (domestic) listing of terrorists?
options: UN Security Council resolution 2231
UN Security Council resolution 1373
UN Security Council resolution 1540
UN Security Council resolution 1718
quiz.explanation: Resolution 1373 requires states to freeze terrorist funds and designate terrorists themselves; ATA section 17 uses its listing criteria. 1718 and 2231 are proliferation regimes; 1540 concerns WMD and non-state actors.

quiz.question: For how long can BFIU order a bank to suspend an account under section 23(1)(c) of the MLPA?
options: Up to 7 days, renewable once
Up to one year, by a single order
Up to 30 days at a time, renewable up to 7 times
Indefinitely, without any review
quiz.explanation: Section 23(1)(c) lets BFIU order suspension or freezing for up to 30 days, and where needed renew it 30 days at a time, up to seven times.

quiz.question: What fine can BFIU impose if a bank ignores its order to suspend an account?
options: Nothing; only a warning is possible
A fixed Tk 10,000
Up to Tk 50,000 on the branch manager only
At least an amount equal to the balance in that account
quiz.explanation: Section 23(6) of the MLPA lets BFIU fine a reporting organisation that fails to comply with a suspension or freezing order at least the balance held in the account.

quiz.question: After receiving a BFIU suspension order on one account, what did BFIU Circular Letter 5 of August 2026 tell banks to do?
options: Inform BFIU without delay of that account's balance and details of other related accounts
Close all of the customer's accounts at the bank and return the balances to him so that BFIU can trace the money
Wait for BFIU to ask before sharing any further information
Notify the customer so that he can appeal to BFIU
quiz.explanation: The circular letter, citing Rule 26(4) of the MLP Rules 2019, asks reporting organisations to inform BFIU promptly of the balance and of related accounts once they receive a suspension order.

quiz.question: Which information must accompany a cross-border wire transfer of USD 1,000 or more sent by Doyel?
options: A copy of the BFIU registration of the receiving bank
Only the beneficiary's name and bank, with no originator details, because the sending bank already holds the originator's KYC
The originator's tax returns for the last three years
Accurate, verified originator information, including an account number or unique transaction reference
quiz.explanation: Circular 26 paragraph 9.1(1) requires accurate (verified) originator information for cross-border wires of USD 1,000 or more, with an account number or unique transaction reference so the payment can be traced.

quiz.question: Who must approve a bank's procedure for preventing and detecting TF and PF transactions?
options: The board of directors
The branch BAMLCOs
The external auditor
BFIU, case by case
quiz.explanation: Circular 26 paragraph 10(1) requires each bank to set up the procedure with the board's approval and issue staff instructions; ATA section 16(2) also places this on the board.

sessions.title: The Bank's Programme: Governance, Training, Audit, Records and Penalties
sessions.summary: Build a programme BFIU would accept: board policy, the CEO's statement, the CCC and CAMLCO, BAMLCOs and quarterly meetings, self-assessment and independent testing, training under paragraph 11.2, record keeping and the penalties for failure.
objectives: Describe the roles of the board, CEO, CCC, CAMLCO, DCAMLCO, BAMLCOs and internal audit
Run the half-yearly self-assessment and independent testing cycle
Apply the training and record-keeping requirements of Circular 26
Explain the fines and other sanctions for banks and responsible staff

cards.title: Six weeks to the inspection
cards.setting: Board meeting room, Doyel Commercial Bank head office, Motijheel. 3:00 pm.

lines.text: BFIU's inspection team arrives in six weeks. Today we check the whole programme, not just the cases.
Md. Rezaul Karim, head of internal audit. My team's independent testing found two branches where fewer than half the officers have had formal AML training.
Agrabad is fine, but our last quarterly branch meeting skipped the sanctions item. I've fixed the agenda.
And the half-yearly CCC report went to BFIU on time? It's due within two months of the half-year end.
It did. But an inspector will ask who sits on the CCC, how often it met, and what the board did with our report.
Final stage: the Board Chamber. Here we prove the programme works, from the board to the branch.

scenes.heading: Board policy
scenes.narration: The board, or the top management committee where applicable, approves the bank's own AML/CFT policy, built on international standards, the laws and BFIU's instructions, and has it reviewed from time to time.

scenes.heading: The CEO's commitment
scenes.narration: Every year the CEO issues a clear statement of commitment to all staff on preventing money laundering and terrorist financing, with directions to put it into practice.

scenes.heading: Central Compliance Committee
scenes.narration: A Central Compliance Committee of at least seven senior members, led by the CAMLCO, sets the programme, meets at least four times a year and reports to the CEO. No internal auditor may sit on it.

scenes.heading: AML division and branches
scenes.narration: The AML & CFT Division, headed by the DCAMLCO, issues instructions to branches. Every branch has a BAMLCO who holds quarterly AML meetings.

scenes.heading: Independent checks
scenes.narration: Branches self-assess every six months, internal audit tests them independently, and the AML division reports the findings up to the CEO and the board, with a copy to BFIU.

items.label: Board
items.detail: Approves the AML/CFT policy and TF/PF procedure; receives the half-yearly CCC report.

items.label: CEO
items.detail: Annual statement of commitment to all staff; directs implementation.

items.label: CCC and CAMLCO
items.detail: At least 7 members; quarterly meetings; CAMLCO no more than two steps below the CEO.

items.label: AML & CFT Division
items.detail: Headed by the DCAMLCO (at least DGM/SVP); issues branch instructions.

items.label: BAMLCOs
items.detail: One in every branch: manager, second officer or experienced senior officer.

cards.title: The half-yearly self-assessment cycle
cards.prompt: Put the steps of Circular 26 paragraph 8 in order.
steps: The branch completes the self-assessment checklist (Annex C) for the half-year
The branch manager chairs a meeting of relevant officers to discuss the draft report
Issues the branch cannot fix are written up and the report goes to internal audit and the AML division
Internal audit reviews the reports and visits any branch where a risky issue appears
The AML division prepares its half-yearly evaluation report for the CEO and board
Progress on the recommendations is discussed at the branch's next quarterly meeting

cards.question: Doyel wants its head of internal audit to sit on the Central Compliance Committee to 'connect the two functions'. What does Circular 26 say?
options: It is required, so audit can sign off CCC decisions
No internal audit officer may be a member of the CCC
It is allowed if the board approves it
Only the deputy head of internal audit may join
cards.explanation: Paragraph 1.3(1)(f) says no internal audit officer can be a CCC member; the CCC and internal audit must carry out their AML/CFT duties completely separately.

cards.title: Training under paragraph 11.2
cards.body:
Circular 26 makes training part of compliance:

- **All officers** must receive suitable ML, TF and PF training: basic AML/CFT training, training on the risks of their own work, targeted by level and department, and **refresher training at intervals**.
- The **CAMLCO, DCAMLCO and other relevant officers** need suitable training and/or a professional certification.
- The bank must **keep training records** (para 11.2(3) and para 12(2)).
